content.confidence: 1: You are unable to assess this paper and have alerted the ACs to seek an opinion from different reviewers.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper studies the theory of gradient optimization and connects classical machine learning and quantum machine learning for this question. The theoretical contributions are the following:
- It points out the universal laziness issues for both settings
- It dervies the theory why optimization still performs well despite laziness (eq 15)
- Finally it studies the settings containing noise, showing an algorithm that is noise resilient
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The paper seems to make interesting and significant connections to something outside classical machine learning (quantum machine learning)
- The paper makes significant theoretical contributions to explain optimization efficiency depiste laziness and derive also theory for noisy cases

Weakness:
- There are some simulations and results, which I think should be put forward (e.g. Figure 2 and Figure 3) to ground the theory; this is more readable for machine learning community.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written although due to the theoretical nature of the paper, it is pretty hard to grasp the content for people not familar with the problems. The theory derived seems both novel and has practical consequences.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper studies optimization efficiency of neural networks (both quantun and classic) despite laziness. The paper derives theoretical insights showing that for overparameterized large width networks, the network can still achieves good optimization performance despite laziness. Following that, the paper also shows that similar insights hold despite noise in the data.

I feel that maybe the paper can be slightly easier to read if the authors put forward simulation results that support the theory.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer DqJm for the positive affirmation of our work, and we modify our work accordingly. Now the paper is significantly changed accordingly.

1). We notice that the comment includes,

"The paper is clearly written although due to the theoretical nature of the paper, it is pretty hard to grasp the content for people not familar with the problems. The theory derived seems both novel and has practical consequences."

Now, a new section (Section 2) has been added to the draft labeled in red, including background knowledge about quantum mechanics, quantum computing, quantum machine learning, noises, k-design theories, comparisons to other related works, and a definition table. Some languages are improved to increase clarity.

2). We notice that the comment includes,

"There are some simulations and results, which I think should be put forward (e.g. Figure 2 and Figure 3) to ground the theory; this is more readable for machine learning community."

"I feel that maybe the paper can be slightly easier to read if the authors put forward simulation results that support the theory."

It is a great idea that one should push further numerical simulations and study the effects of noises, despite the theoretical nature of the paper. However, since the Appendix is technical, we do not hope to move the old Figure 2 and Figure 3 toward the main text. But we add a new numerical simulation in the current Figure 2 of the draft to show the noise resilience and robustness of the paper. Further numerical results are shown in some companion papers, and due to the double-blind nature of the review process, we cannot exhibit them here.

We believe that now the work has been improved further and satisfies the criteria of the Reviewer.

content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work considers the gradient descent dynamics for random variational quantum circuits. Its main contribution is to draw a distinction between the *barren plateau* phenomenon - which is the observation by [McClean et al. '18] that the fraction of quantum states falling outside a fixed angular distance from zero decreases exponentially in the Hilbert space dimension, implying that quantum observables concentrate leading to an exponentially small gradient - and *laziness*, the phenomenon in which the weights of classical overparametrised neural networks stay close to their initialisation, leading to the NTK regime of neural networks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I am not familiar with the quantum machine learning literature, and overall I found this manuscript hard to parse for a non-expert. The main contributions are not clearly stated, the concepts are introduced in a disordered way, and most of the statements involve back of the envelope approximations and scaling arguments which are hard to follow if you don't previously know them. Given that the work is only 7 pages, the authors could have made the use of the extra space to make the paper more accessible to the general machine learning public. I remind the authors the that most of the ICLR community is not aware of what a "variational angle" and a "2-design" random average are!

As I questioned myself whether my problem following the results was my ignorance in the field or the way the work is framed, I browsed the related work literature and came across with the concurrent works of [Abedi et al. (2022); Anschuetz & Kiani (2022)], which despite containing a similar discussion on the landscape of quantum variational circuits and the distinction between lazy training and barren plateau, are much easier to parse.

Finally, note that the term "lazy training" has been introduced by [Chizat et al. (2019)], where it was also shown it is crucially connected to the scale of the network at initialisation.

**Small typos**:
- Page 3, "learn ing" -> learning

**References**:

[[Abedi et al. (2022)]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.08232.pdf) Erfan Abedi, Salman Beigi, Leila Taghavi. *Quantum lazy training*. arXiv: 2202.08232 [quant-ph]

[[Anschuetz & Kiani (2022)]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05786). Eric R. Anschuetz, Bobak T. Kiani. *Beyond Barren Plateaus: Quantum Variational Algorithms Are Swamped With Traps*. arXiv: 2205.05786 [quant-ph]

[[Chizat et al. (2019)]](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2019/hash/ae614c557843b1df326cb29c57225459-Abstract.html) L. Chizat, E. Oyallon, and F. Bach. *On lazy training in differentiable programming*. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 32, 2019.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The manuscript has serious problems regarding clarity and reproducibility: the main contributions are not clearly stated, many of the quantities used are not defined and the authors abuse of approximations which are not justified. Regarding novelty, the manuscript seems to overlap with some works in the literature, although given the submission dates they can be considered concurrent.
content.summary_of_the_review: As a non-expert in the quantum machine learning literature, I found this work hard to parse. After reading some related works, I concluded this is in big part a problem of the submission. In its current form I believe this manuscript is going to be cryptic to a big part of the ICLR community. Note I am open to changing my mind, since I believe there is a lot of room for improving the exposition in the manuscript.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1127 by Reviewer gg18

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper uses an analytical framework based on a quantum neural tangent kernel (QNTK) framework to study the gradient dynamics of variational quantum circuits (VQCs) during training, and connects this to the study of barren plateaus. The introduction of a simple noise model allows the authors to demonstrate that gradient based training of VQCs can reach robust minimum loss values in the presence of noise.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ The authors develop an interesting analogy between the width of a classical neural networks and the Hilbert space dimension of a VQC, and argue that a formal version of the barren plateau problem emerges also in large-width neural networks.

+ The authors extend previous results showing the success of gradient descent in overparameterized noiseless VQCs to the setting of an idealized noise model. Within this model, the quality of the final loss value depends in a straightforward way on the extent of the noise, a useful result.

- The overparameterized regime in which the results start to ensure performance or robustness of the trained model require the parameter count to be comparable to the Hilbert space dimension. Given that the former must fit on a classical computer to train the VQC, while the latter must be too large to store on a classical computer to ensure any form of quantum advantage with the VQC, it doesn't feel like the papers findings have much immediate practical value.

- The discussion of laziness, precision, and barren plateaus feels less convincing, and I think the paper would be easier to read if much of this were dropped.

- Overall, the paper feels harder to read than it should be, and more work can be done on creating an effective summary of the high-level findings for casual readers. On a completely subjective level, I found the similar results of [Anschuetz & Kiani (2022)] to be presented in a way that made them more immediately interpretable.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* Although many of the analytic results used here were previously developed in [Liu et al. (2021a)] and [Liu et al. (2022)], the new results do have some qualitative value for understanding the role of parameterization on trainability.

* One point I was unsure of during reading is whether Figure 1 is based on actual instances of VQCs, or is it more akin to an "artist's rendition" of under- and over-parameterized loss landscapes? If it is the latter (as the caption suggests), I would encourage the authors to use a figure that is derived from the loss landscape of a real PQCs, for example via a projection onto a 2D subspace.

* As a minor point, Eqs. (5) and (6) (and the sentence preceding each) are duplicates of each other, and one of them should be removed.
content.summary_of_the_review: The results are interesting and novel, but seem to have limited practical utility, with room for improvement in the presentation.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1127 by Reviewer gg18

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer gg18 for the positive affirmation of our work, and we modify our work according to the comments. Now the paper is significantly changed accordingly.
We notice that the comment includes,

1). "Given that the former must fit on a classical computer to train the VQC, while the latter must be too large to store on a classical computer to ensure any form of quantum advantage with the VQC, it doesn't feel like the papers findings have much immediate practical value." "The results are interesting and novel, but seem to have limited practical utility"

We agree with the statement that, indeed, the setup is theoretical since it requires the training parameters to be comparable to the dimension of Hilbert space. However, as a theoretical result, it has its own value, similar to the introduction of infinite-width neural networks in the classical machine-learning community. Moreover, we discuss the effect of noises in our paper, and show that our overparametrized quantum neural networks are noise-resilient. The introduction of noises makes our work more practical. Finally, we comment on the practical usage of the QNTK theory. For instance, since we know that higher QNTKs will lead to faster convergences, one can make plots at initialization about the value of the QNTK eigenvalues for different variational angles. Thus, one could choose larger QNTK initializations at the beginning of training, and in practice, it might lead to better convergence. Moreover, there are relationships between the NTK eigenvalues, generalization error, and alignments, where our results might be helpful in improving the generalization properties of quantum machine learning models. We make comments on this point labeled in red in Section 5 in the current draft.

2). "Overall, the paper feels harder to read than it should be, and more work can be done on creating an effective summary of the high-level findings for casual readers. On a completely subjective level, I found the similar results of [Anschuetz & Kiani (2022)] to be presented in a way that made them more immediately interpretable." "with room for improvement in the presentation." "The discussion of laziness, precision, and barren plateaus feels less convincing, and I think the paper would be easier to read if much of this were dropped."

Now, a new section (section 2 in the current draft) has been added to the draft labeled in red, including background knowledge about quantum mechanics, quantum computing, quantum machine learning, noises, k-design theories, comparisons to other related works, and a definition table. New numerical results are added to support the claim of the authors (Figure 2 in the current draft), and some languages are improved to increase clarity. Moreover, a comparison to [Anschuetz & Kiani (2022)] is added in the current draft. We believe that now the work has been improved further and satisfies the criteria of the Reviewer.

Moreover, the claims about laziness, precision and barren plateaus are conceptual interpretations and are original. We believe that based on the current draft, the conclusion is manifest and convincing enough for the reader.

3). "One point I was unsure of during reading is whether Figure 1 is based on actual instances of VQCs, or is it more akin to an "artist's rendition" of under- and over-parameterized loss landscapes? If it is the latter (as the caption suggests), I would encourage the authors to use a figure that is derived from the loss landscape of a real PQCs, for example via a projection onto a 2D subspace."

Figure 1 is indeed an artistic illustration. Practical paintings are hard to make in this case, since the loss landscape exists in a very high dimension, and we find that only printing cross sections are confusing to show our findings. For instance, if there is only a cross section, the same point in the 2D plot will represent multiple different loss values, so it is hard to visualize. We add comments on the draft that maybe a good data compression and visualization will solve the problem, and cite the reference for visualization tools.

4). "As a minor point, Eqs. (5) and (6) (and the sentence preceding each) are duplicates of each other, and one of them should be removed."

Good catch. Now it is modified.

We again appreciate the Reviewer's comments, and they are very helpful for us in improving the paper. We believe that the current format of the paper will satisfy the requirement of ICLR.
